findings.title: Acquisition, mercy, and claimed lineage
findings.claim: The focus reports a creaturely act of taking a child and attributes it to al-Rahman. Wider passages answer the same child-taking formula through creation by command, describe mercy alongside divine self-sufficiency, and identify the attribution as false; the claim therefore reads as creaturely lineage projected onto a merciful creator.
findings.mechanism: The focus verb for taking carries the alleged acquisition, while the child noun supplies its lineage object and al-Rahman supplies the divine title. The wider 19:35 passage denies taking a child and frames creation through the command 'Be'; 6:133 puts mercy beside self-sufficiency; 18:4-5 repeats the son claim and calls it an ungrounded false utterance; 21:26 repeats the same formula before describing honored servants. These contacts return through the focus's taking, speech, title, and child words, changing the allegation from a bare relation into a creaturely model set against command, mercy, and servanthood.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see how the alleged child relation carries a view of divine identity: it imports human acquisition and lineage into a title associated with mercy, while wider passages keep creation and honored service in view.
findings.containment: The focus still reports what people said; these wider passages qualify the claim without establishing every speaker's motive or a full doctrine. Target morphology is not supplied, and the comparison does not state a causal account beyond the cited wording.

epistemic.reason: The publication's focus anchors map to the supplied branches, and the cited connections provide exact wider Arabic. The interpretation remains qualified because connection targets lack morphology and some of the relation is cross-context synthesis.

The wider 19:33 text states Jesus' birth, while 19:35 denies divine child-taking and describes creation through the command 'Be'; the focus child word returns through both contacts. The birth branch supplies a human event, and the production branch can only be reached by analogy, so the two wider contexts distinguish human descent from commanded origination.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the child claim against both a stated human birth and a different account of divine origination, without losing the ordinary offspring meaning of the focus word.
findings.containment: The focus surface selects a child or offspring. The birth context says Jesus was born but does not name the mother's action, and the production branch excludes direct human descent except by general analogy. Neither branch changes walad into a word for creation, and the wider texts do not state the speakers' motive.

epistemic.reason: The Arabic targets and focus root range support the contact, but target morphology is unavailable and the production branch applies only through an expressly bounded analogy.
